The Soviet Union was communist, not socialist. Socialism and capitalism are a million times closer than communism is to either. Communism means everybody gets the same. There is no merit, there is no reward for excellence. The greatest difference between socialism and capitalism is that socialism, in its most extreme form, has government control over socially critical services. So for instance instead of having the excellence of Time Warner and Comcast running the internet, it'd probably be a government service like fire fighting that is "freely" (you obviously still pay for it through your taxes) for everybody. There's also generally an implicit social safety net in socialism. Today we view many corporations as too big to let fail. In socialism we would instead consider people too small to let fail. So even if you suck at capitalism you still end up with the basics needed for life and to try to get back on your feet again.

But where capitalism/socialism and communism really diverge is in rewards for excellence. There is no cap. In socialism if you do well for yourself and produce a desired valuable service you can become a billionaire - same as capitalism. There would be higher tax rates so as you get richer it gets harder and harder to get even richer still, but there'd also be fewer taxes on the way up there. Basically it becomes much easier to go from poor to rich, but much harder to go from rich to absurdly ultra mega rich.

I think the direction the US is headed is probably towards a basic income strapped into more or less our current system. The number of employees required is already dropping and globalism means companies are able to grab talent from across the world instead of just our little continent which is further having a shrinking effect on total required employment per-country. And of course automation will turn all this up to 11. You end up with a simple problem. Companies don't need employees to make their product, but they do need people to buy their product. Consumers need a money to buy the product, but no longer have jobs to earn money. Put two and two together and a basic income keeps things flowing pretty well while also conveniently solving lots of little issues like poverty, petty need-based crime, hunger, and so on.
